text.p: Prudential Corp, Britain's biggest life insurance company, could do better than a rumoured merger with banking giant National Westminster, analysts said on Monday, and the stock market indicated such a marriage would not happen.
The Pru has made no secret of the fact that it would like to extend its distribution possibilities but analysts say the Pru could achieve its desire without taking on NatWest with all its baggage.

Analysts say other firms that would make better merger partners for the Pru include the still mutually owned Nationwide Building Society, the Abbey National, which was recently approached by NatWest, and even the recently floated Halifax, Britain's biggest mortgage lender.

These companies would be interested in expanding their insurance and long-term savings capabilities but would not bring with them NatWest's problems of heavy involvement in corporate banking and, more importantly, its beleaguered investment banking unit NatWest Markets.

NatWest is in the process of reviewing its strategy at the investment bank after the unit reported a 90 million pounds ($150 million) loss on interest rate options earlier this year which led to the departure of its chief executive and other senior managers.

Prudential is unlikely to have been keen on taking on a business that produces such low returns but with NatWest rumoured to be planning a reorganisation which would put all corporate banking and treasury activity back in the commercial bank, some feel that this might have led to a sale of the residue.

"A merger between Prudential and NatWest would fill a very noticeable gap for NatWest but one of the reasons it might not work is that it would produce very little cost saving," said one analyst who declined to be named.

The talks between NatWest and the Pru are also thought to have foundered on who would end up running the merged business with the NatWest board apparently unwilling to accept Prudential chief Sir Peter Davis at the helm rather than its own chief executive Derek Wanless.
Shares in Natwest were 14.5 pence lower at 852 with analysts saying this showed the market did not believe a merger was likely.
"I would have expected the price to have held up a bit better if the market thought this was going to happen," said David Poutney at Panmure Gordon.

Analysts say it is becoming more and more difficult to see NatWest pulling off a successful merger. The bank put itself in play earlier this year when it approached Abbey National for merger talks but was rebuffed.
Since then it has been linked with many other companies including Barclays and Royal Bank of Scotland.

"It's hard to see where a merger could happen now," said another analyst. "If the market begins to feel that then you could see the NatWest share price come off," he said, noting that NatWest had outperformed the banking sector by around eight percent since it came into play.
But other analysts see no bid premium in the current NatWest price and see some continued upside in the stock on a fundamental basis.
Neither the Pru nor NatWest would make any comment on the rumours. ($ = 0.595 British Pounds)
